bellum, bellī n.

noun, second declension

To wage war, bellum gerere; to make war on, bellum īnferre with the dative; to declare war, bellum indīcere, the regular expression (Lewis & Short). The verbs of war are set phrases: bellum indīcere declares it, bellum īnferre (with the dative) starts it against someone, bellum gerere wages it, bellum cōnficere brings it to a winning end, bellum compōnere ends it by agreement (Lewis & Short s.v. bellum). Of the phrases below, bellī initium facere, bellī fīnem facere, bellī tempore, bellum clandestīnum and bellī sēdēs are not found in Lewis & Short or the loci collections; the words are classical. A guerrilla war is a modern idea: clandestīnus is classically “secret, hidden”.

Examples

  • In amōre haec omnia īnsunt vitia: injūriae, suspīciōnēs, inimīcitiae, indūtiae, bellum, pāx rūrsum.

    Love has all these troubles in it: wrongs, suspicions, quarrels, truces, war, then peace again.Ter. Eun. 59–61

  • Diū adparandum est bellum, ut vincās celerius.

    Prepare long for a war, so that you win it sooner.Publil. Syr. D 3
